passages.t: Eliphaz: the innocent do not perish
passages.happening:
‘Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied’ (verse 1). He begins gently: “If one ventures a word with you, will you be wearied? Yet who can keep from speaking?” (verse 2).

He reminds Job of the man he used to be. “Your words have steadied those who stumbled; you have braced the knees that were buckling” (verse 4). Now trouble has come to Job, and he is dismayed. “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” (verse 6).

Then the principle: “Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (verse 7). He has seen that those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish. Even the fiercest lions have their teeth broken, and their cubs are scattered.
passages.hearers:
Eliphaz speaks first, probably as the eldest and most respected. He comes from Teman in Edom, a land known for its wise men. He is not cruel. He truly tries to comfort, and he begins by honoring Job's past kindness to others.

His view of justice was widely held in the ancient world. Wisdom writings in Egypt and Mesopotamia taught that the gods reward the righteous and punish the wicked, and Israel's Proverbs teach the same pattern as a general truth. Put in the form Eliphaz would sign, his case is this: God is just, the world is morally ordered, and the righteous are not destroyed. So Job should take heart, trust his own piety, and wait for God to set things right.

But his question in verse 7 assumes its own answer. The reader knows from chapters 1 and 2 that Job is exactly the innocent man Eliphaz says does not suffer. A gentle start hides a hard conclusion: if Job is suffering, perhaps he is not as innocent as he seems.

The lion was a common picture of the powerful wicked, fierce and seemingly unbeatable, and yet broken in the end.
passages.later: Edom's wisdom was famous enough for the prophets to name it: “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent?” (Jeremiah 49:7).
passages.hard:
Eliphaz says many true things. Why does God later say the friends did not speak rightly?

Much of what Eliphaz says is true in general. God opposes the wicked, human beings are frail, and no one is perfectly righteous before God. Proverbs and the Psalms say similar things. The problem is that Eliphaz treats a general pattern as a strict rule and applies it to Job without knowing the facts. He reasons backward, from suffering to sin. Because Job is suffering, he assumes, Job must have done something to deserve it. The book shows through its prologue that this is false in Job's case.

The lesson is not that the friends' ideas are wholly false. Paul quotes Eliphaz's words in 1 Corinthians 3:19 as Scripture. It is that true ideas misapplied can wound and mislead. No one may take a sentence like verse 7 and say it to a person in grief, as if their loss proved their guilt. That is what Eliphaz did, and God called it speaking wrongly of him (42:7).
passages.asks: Eliphaz remembered how Job had helped others, and then failed to help him. Ask whether you find it easier to give comfort than to receive it. And ask whether you have ever answered someone's pain with a principle instead of with yourself.

passages.happening:
Eliphaz claims a revelation. “Now a word came to me secretly; my ears caught a whisper of it” (verse 12). It came in visions of the night, when deep sleep falls. Fear and trembling seized him, a spirit glided past his face, and the hair on his body stood up. A form stood before him that he could not make out, and he heard a voice.

Its message: “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (verse 17). If God does not trust even his servants, and charges his angels with error, how much less those ‘who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundations are in the dust’ (verse 19). People are crushed like a moth and perish unnoticed, and they die without wisdom.
passages.hearers:
Night visions and dreams were widely thought to be channels of divine messages. The details Eliphaz gives, the trembling, the shaking bones, the hair standing on end, the half-seen form and the whispering voice, are meant to give his message authority. The word for deep sleep, tardemah, is the word used of the sleep God sent on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and on Abram (Genesis 15:12).

The message itself is true. No human being is perfectly righteous before God. People are made from the dust and are frail. But Eliphaz uses it as a reason to assume that Job's suffering must answer to some hidden fault. Frailty is not the same as guilt, and the book will show the difference.

Eliphaz's claim of a private revelation makes his error more serious. He is not only giving advice; he is speaking for God.
passages.later: The picture of houses of clay goes back to the making of the first man: ‘Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils’ (Genesis 2:7).
passages.asks: Eliphaz said a true thing in a way that made it a weapon. Ask whether you have used something true about God to close a conversation rather than to open one. And ask how you test a word that comes to you in God's name before you pass it on.
